3. Thereafter the appellant filed an application on 28.04.2010 in Title Suit no. 1633 of 2008 for staying the further proceedings of the said title suit tell disposal of the First Miscellaneous Appeal no. 275 of 2009 contending inter alia that one Shib Prashad Ghosh appointed guardian of said Swaraj Chandra Ghosh and filed written statement where he mentioned that the defendant no. 1 Swaraj Chandra Ghosh is a lunatic person since 2005 but the defendant no. 1 sold some property to one Md. Abu Taher by a registered saf-kabala deed no. 8281 dated 26.12.2007 and after coming to the knowledge about the order of appointment of guardian dated 30.04.2009 the sole appellant has filed this First Miscellaneous Appeal no. 275 of 2009 before the honorable High Court Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh which is pending and as such till disposal of the said First Miscellaneous Appeal the further proceedings of the title suit no. 1633 of 2008 may kindly be stayed. 

 "The elaborate procedure laid down by the Legislature for conducting an inquiry into the matter must be strictly followed. The court should not consider itself relieved of the responsibility by the mere circumstances that some or all of the relatives of the person concerned have declared that he is a lunatic. The court ought to form its own independent judgment on the point". 

 "As regards the preliminary objection, I think it has no force. Appeal lies to the High Court under section 33 of the Act, which is to the following effect: 

 "83 An appeal shall lie to the High Court from any order made by a District Court under this Chapter." 

 13. Chapter V deals with proceedings in lunacy outside Presidency Towns. It contains Section 62 to section 83. The order under appeal was passed under section 65(2) of the Act and therefore, an appeal against an order under section 65(2) will lie to the High Court. Section 83 does not speak or specify the person or persons who can appeal under section 83 from such an order. Section 83 is in general terms conferring the right of appeal from any order passed by a District Court, which, in the recent case. In view of section, 2(2) of the Act, which definite "District Court" is the District Judge of the District. When the person who is to appeal under section 83 is not specifically mentioned therein, it means that any person, who is a party to the Lunacy Case and who is aggrieved by any order passed under chapter V of the Act, is entitled to appeal. It is true that in Joshi Ram Krishan V. Mt. Rukmini Bai, AIII 1949 All 449-ILR (1950) All 396 relied upon by Mr. Ray, the appellant was the lunatic himself; but that does not mean that only the lunatic has the right to appeal under section 83 of the Act. In my opinion, any person, who is aggrieved by any order passed under Chapter V of the Act by a District Judge has the right to appeal against such order to the High Court under section 83. No doubt, the lunatic is the most aggrieved person, but he being a lunatic, is not capable of understanding the legal implication of the order under appeal and, therefore he is not expected to file an appeal objectors were interested in getting Chaturbhuj Singh declared not lunatic, because they had earlier got a gift executed in their favour by Chaturbhuj Singh. It is obvious, therefore, that the objectors also aggrieved by the order under appeal and as such, they had the right in appeal under section 83 of the Act. I therefore, hold that the appeal by this objectors appellants is maintainable". 

 15. It is very much pertinent before arriving to a definite finding the provisions of law as contain in section 62 of the Lunacy Act 1912 where it contains that whenever any person is possessed of property and is alleged to be a Lunatic the District Court within whose jurisdiction such person is residing may upon application by order direct an in question for the purpose of ascertaining whether such person is of unsound mind and incapable of managing himself and his affairs. In the said Act it also provides that application for such inquisition may be made by any relative of the alleged Lunatic or by any public curator appointed under the Succession Act 1925 hereinafter referred to as the curator or by the Government pleader as defined in the Code of Civil Procedure 1908 or if the property of the alleged Lunatic consists in whole or in part of land or any interest in land by the collector of the District in which it is situate. If the property or any part there is of such a description that it would subject the proprietor, if disqualified; to the jurisdiction of the court of Wards, the application may be made by the collector on behalf of the court of Wards. 

 16. The provisions of sections 40, 41 and 42 shall regulate the proceedings of the District Court with regard to the matters to which they relate. 

 17. The District Court, if it thinks fit may appoint two or more persons to act as assessors to the court in the said in question relates is of unsound mind so as to be incapable of managing his affairs but that he is capable of managing his affairs but that he is capable of managing himself and is not dangerous to himself or to others, the court may make such orders as it thinks fit for the management of the estate of the Lunatic including proper provisions for the maintenance of the lunatic and of such members of his family as are dependant on him for maintenance but it shall not be necessary to make any order as to the custody of the person of the Lunatic. 

 18. If the estate of a lunatic so found or any part there of consists of property which by the law for the time being in force subjects the proprietor, if his qualified to the jurisdiction of the court of wards shall be authorized to take charge of the same. 

 19. If the estate of a lunatic so found consists in whole or in part of land or any interest in land but is not of such a nature that it would subject the proprietor, if disqualified to the jurisdiction of the court of Wards the District Court may direct the collector to take charge of the person and estate of the lunatic. 

 21. The collector shall thereupon appoint a manager of the estate and may appoint a guardian of the person of the lunatic. Upon the completion of the in question the court shall determine whether the alleged lunatic is of unsound mind and incapable of managing himself and his affairs or may come to a special finding that such alleged lunatic is of unsound mind so as to be incapable of managing his affairs but that he is capable of managing himself and is not dangerous to himself or to others. 

 22. 66(1) If the alleged lunatic resides at a distance of more than fifty miles from the place where the District Court is held to which the application is made the said court may issue a commission to any subordinate court to make the in question and such subordinate court shall thereupon conduct the in question in the manner hereinbefore provided in this chapter. 

 (2) On the completion of the in question the subordinate court shall transmit the record of the proceedings with the opinion of the assessors if assessor have been appointed and in its own motion on the case and the District Court shall thereupon proceed to dispose of the application in the manner provided in section 65, subsection (2). 

 23. Provided that the District court may direct the subordinate court to make such further or other inquiries as it thinks fit before disposing of the application. 

 67(1) The court may make orders for the custody of lunatics so found by in question and the management of their estates. 

 24. In all other cases the District Court shall appoint a manager of the estate of the lunatic and may appoint a guardian of his person. Provided that as District Court may instead of appointing a manager of the estate of a lunatic exercise any of the powers conferred on the High Court Division under section 56 and 59. 

 25. Any person who has been appointed by the District Court or collector to manage the estate of a lunatic shall if so required enter into a found in such form and with such sureties as to the court or the collector as the case may be may seem fit, engaging duly to account for what her may receive in respect of the property of the lunatic. 

 26. Now let explain the provisions of law as described in the case of Sarjug Singh .. Vs.. Tulabo Kuer reported in AIR Patna 1969 page 33 where his lordship of Patna High Court nicely explained the meaning the word `Lunacy' His lordship held that:- 

 27. I think it has no force. Appeal lies to the High Court under section 83 of the Lunacy Act, which is to the following effect "83 An appeal shall be to the High Court from any order made by a District Court under this chapter. The order under Appeal was passed under section 65(20 of the Act and therefore an appeal against an order under section 65(2) will be to the High Court. Section 83 does not speak or specify the person or persons who can appeal under section 83 from such an order section 83 is in general serous conferring the right of appeal from any order passed by District Court , which in the recent case in view of section 2(2) of the Act which defines "District. When the person who is to appeal under section 83 is not specifically mentioned therein, it means that any person, who is a party to the Lunacy case and who is aggrieved by any order passed under chapter V of the Act is entitled to appeal. It is true that in Joshi Ram Krishan ..Vs.. Md. Rukmini Bai, AIR 1949 Act 449 relied upon by Mr. Ray the appellant was a lunatic himself but that does not mean' that only the lunatic has the right to appeal under section 83 of the Act. In my opinion any person who is aggrieved by any order passed under chapter V of the Act by a District Court has the right to appeal against such order to the High court under section 83. No doubt, the lunatic is the most aggrieved person but he being a lunatic is not capable of under standing the legal in implication of the order under appeal and therefore he is not expected to file an appeal. Objectors were interested in getting chaterjheej Singh declared not lunatic because they had earlier got .a gift executed in their favour by chatetjheej Singh. It is obvious therefore that the objectors also aggrieved by the order under, appeal and as such they had the right to appeal under section 83 of the Act. It therefore hold that the appeal by objectors appellants is maintainable. 

 28. On similar point our High Court decided in the case of Habibullah ..Vs.. Solem Rahman reported in 12 DLR page 441 where his lordship held that "In assuming jurisdiction under the lunacy Act the court must keep in view the distinction between mere weakness of intellect and lunacy as understood in the act. It is only with lunatics as defined in section 3(5) that the Act is concerned. It is therefore the duty of the court before proceeding further to determine judicially whether the person alleged to be incapable of managing himself or his affairs is really a lunatic in this since. The finding has got very far reaching consequences and must be given after very great care and deliberation. 

 29. The elaborate procedure laid down by the legislature for conducting and inquiry into the matter must be strictly followed. The court should not consider itself relieved of the responsibility by the mere circumstance that some or all of the relatives of the person concerned have declared that he is a lunatic the court ought to form its own independent judgment on the point. 

 33. Send down the lower courts record along with a copy of this judgment to the concern court forthwith for information and necessary action.
